newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's MRTA says unlikely to win full hostage demand.
newsitem.headline: Peru's MRTA says unlikely to win full hostage demand.

text.p: A senior leader of Peru's Marxist rebel movement MRTA, holding 72 hostages in Lima, revealed that the group accepts it is unlikely to win its central demand for the release of all its jailed comrades.

In an interview earlier this week at a secret jungle location, the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement said publicly for the first time its spectacular takeover of the Japanese ambassador's home would probably not achieve its prime objective.
"I do not think all of the 400-plus (jailed comrades) are going to get out," said a man who identified himself as "Comrade Alejandro," a member of the MRTA's high-command.
He said the MRTA was prepared to negotiate how many comrades should be freed depending on their experience and importance in the movement.

The MRTA hostage-takers in Lima have repeatedly said they will never give up their main demand, but the start last week of face-to-face talks with the government raised speculation that they might shift their position.

The interview -- the first such contact with the media since the Dec. 17 hostage-taking -- took place in the group's military heartland at a peasant's wooden shack, overlooking the steamy jungle of eastern Peru. It was a day's travel by truck and on foot in the county of Junin, 200 miles (320 km) east of Lima.
Dressed in olive fatigues, a green peaked cap, sunglasses and rubber rainboots, the short rebel, who looked in his mid-30's, smoked and cradled his polished AKM rifle as he spoke.
In negotiations with the government, Nestor Cerpa Cartolini, the leader of the Lima attack, had ultimate responsibility, Comrade Alejandro said.

But the MRTA's high-command, made up of four regional heads and the group's "most outstanding comrades," had originally agreed on a set of objectives for the mission and kept in regular contact with the rebels inside the diplomatic mansion, he added.
Asked if Cerpa would ever drop completely the rebels' demand for the release of jailed comrades, the jungle commander said, "I do not think so."

He also said the government still had to address other rebel demands, including ransom payment for the hostages' release. He knew of no payments made so far in return for the freeing of hundreds of captives in the first few weeks of the 64-day siege.

With no sign that talks in Lima were leading to a solution to the crisis any time soon, the military leader held out little hope for new hostage releases. "There are not going to be more (releases). We have made too many goodwill gestures," he said.

In negotiations with the MRTA, the government has floated the possibility of exile for the hostage takers if they relaese their captives unharmed. But Comrade Alejandro said: "The idea does not excite us."

If all of the rebels inside the residence are killed or imprisoned, "we are capable of carrying on," said Alejandro, who was guarded by one armed rebel while others hid in the dense growth watching for possible intruders.
And if there is an attack on the diplomatic mansion, the MRTA "has to make a military response," he added, without elaborating.
He said there were at least 23 rebels inside, while the government claims there are about 15.

Since the assault, the MRTA has noted more Peruvian soldiers in the jungle, but "it seems they are working more on intelligence matters," he said, adding the interview was held one and a half hours on foot from the nearest military base.
The MRTA clashes with the Peruvian army once a month on average, he said. About a third of the fighting force are women and the youngest members are just 16 years old.
Alejandro claimed he was the leader of the one zone in Peru where the MRTA has a permanent military presence. Its military power base was in the three provinces of Oxapampa, Chanchamayo and Satipo.
But he said his region covered more than 22,500 square miles (60,000 square km), encompassing the counties of Junin, Huancavelica and part of Pasco in central Peru.
Refusing to reveal the number of active fighters -- estimated by analysts at no more than 200 -- he said the MRTA is "large enough to make them (the army) feel we exist."
He also claimed the group's structure meant its influence was far-reaching.

Its army received the support of up to 70 percent of the villagers in his central region and civilian "militia" members also helped in minor operations such as robbing food from passing trucks, he said.
The group also had active members working unannounced in community social and labour organisations throughout the country.
He said the MRTA's strength lay in the support of the people in the zone, without whose "collaboration" the rebels could not exist.

The sight of armed rebels riding atop trucks or trekking along muddy paths by moonlight does not phase jungle peasants. Over two days accompanying the MRTA, a Reuters correspondent saw the villagers provide the rebels with transportion, food and lodging as well as hiding packages from possible army checks.
"We encounter no determined resistance. Some help us out of fear, others do it with good faith," Alejandro said.
